Why I Started Echo

I was working with a team on a research project exploring specialized AI models for healthcare administration. We needed to speak with industry professionals, researchers, and technical decision-makers to better understand their workflows and challenges.

Getting people to agree to interviews wasn't necessarily the problem. Finding time on their calendars was.

Some people offered to send voice notes answering our questions instead. That seemed like a practical workaround until I started listening to their responses. Sometimes someone would mention something interesting I wanted to explore further. Other times, an answer raised more questions than it answered.

In a normal interview, I'd simply ask a follow-up. With voice notes, that wasn't as straightforward.

So I started wondering: why couldn't I send someone a link on WhatsApp, let them answer whenever they had time, and still have the kind of back-and-forth I'd get in a live interview?

That's how Echo started. I wasn't trying to build a research platform. I just wanted to solve a problem we kept running into.

What I Built

Echo is an AI interviewer that conducts research conversations through WhatsApp.

I provide the interview questions and research objectives. Echo asks the questions, processes voice-note or text responses, and uses conversational pathways to determine when to probe deeper, ask for clarification, or move to the next topic.

It also transcribes and organizes the conversations so I can review the responses without manually piecing together multiple voice notes.

My Role

I designed the interview experience, from participant invitations to how completed interviews would be reviewed.

The most interesting challenge was designing the conversational pathways. I needed Echo to recognize when an answer deserved a follow-up without getting stuck asking unnecessary questions.

I also worked through consent, interview pauses, conversation memory, and participant controls.

Using AI coding tools, I built the backend and researcher workspace while learning more about APIs, agent architecture, and software development.

One important design decision was separating the AI's judgment from the application's rules. The AI interprets responses and recommends questions, while the application controls consent, interview progress, and message delivery.

Results & Learnings

We've since used Echo to conduct interviews across the different ideas our team is exploring.

What previously took roughly two weeks of coordinating schedules, chasing responses, and conducting interviews now takes less than three days.

Participants can respond when it's convenient for them, and we can review the transcripts without manually transcribing each conversation.

Echo has been tested through a working WhatsApp integration, including voice-note transcription, follow-up questions, consent, pause and resume, and interview completion. I also added automated tests for the interview flow, access controls, invitations, and data deletion.

The experience has taught me a lot about building with AI, particularly the importance of combining flexible model behavior with clear application rules.

There's still work to do around evaluating interview quality across different scenarios, but Echo has already solved the problem I originally built it for.
